citation.title: A Note on Dropping Experimental Subjects who Fail a Manipulation Check

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 2, p. 573 (PDF p. 2)] “Suppose we have an i.i.d. sample from $(Y, S, Z)$, where $Y$ denotes the subject's response, $S$ denotes the result of a manipulation check (1 if the subject passed, 0 if the subject failed), and $Z$ denotes the subject's treatment assignment (1 for treatment 1, 2 for treatment 2, . . .). Without loss of generality, assume that the support of $Z$ is $\{1, \ldots, K\}$, where $K$ is finite. We make three assumptions to proceed. First, we assume that both potential responses and potential results from the manipulation check are stable, by invoking SUTVA (Rubin 1980), which implies both no interference between units and no multiple unobserved versions of the treatment.” [p. 573] ASSUMPTION 1 (SUTVA). $Y = \sum_{z=1}^{K} Y(z)\mathbf{I}(Z = z)$ and $S = \sum_{z=1}^{K} S(z)\mathbf{I}(Z = z)$. [p. 573] “Second, we assume that the treatment is not systematically related to potential outcomes or potential manipulation check results, as would be ensured by random assignment of the treatment.” [p. 574 (PDF p. 3)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Ignorability). For all $z \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, $(Y(z), S(z)) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$, with $\Pr(Z = z) > 0$. “Assumption 2 can be ensured at the design stage by randomizing treatment assignment across subjects.” [p. 574] “Finally, we require that at least some subjects pass the manipulation check in both treatment and control.” ASSUMPTION 3 (Nonzero Passing Rates). For all $z \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, $\Pr[S|Z = z] > 0$. “Note that Assumption 3 is verifiable from the experimental data.” [As printed the event is missing; $\Pr[S = 1|Z = z] > 0$ is meant (finding P010-N002, corrected in P010-T17). Every target uses the corrected form.] [Regularity: Section 2.1, p. 574] “As we proceed, plug-in estimators will be consistent given suitable regularity conditions (e.g., finite third moments, continuity), with the bootstrap providing a basis for asymptotic inference.” [The paper puts no moment condition inside its numbered results. Each conditional mean written in a target is taken to exist; finite first moments of $Y(1), \ldots, Y(K)$ ensure this.] [Target parameter: Section 2.1, p. 574] “Here we consider one possible target that seems natural: $\mathrm{E}[Y(z) - Y(z')|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$, or the average treatment effect among subjects who would pass under all treatment conditions.” [Covariates: Section 2.3, p. 576 (PDF p. 5)] “Suppose that we had a vector of covariates $\mathbf{X}$ associated with each unit, so that we now have an i.i.d. sample from $(Y, S, Z, \mathbf{X})$. We can now write an assumption analogous to Assumption 2.” ASSUMPTION 4 (Ignorability with Covariates). For all $z \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, $(Y(z), S(z), \mathbf{X}) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$, with $\Pr(Z = z) > 0$. [Notation] $Y(z)$ and $S(z)$ are the potential response and the potential result of the manipulation check under treatment $z$; the paper introduces them only through Assumption 1. $\mathrm{E}$ and $\Pr$ refer to the joint law of one draw $(Y(1), \ldots, Y(K), S(1), \ldots, S(K), Z)$ (with $\mathbf{X}$ in Section 2.3), of which $(Y, S, Z)$ is the observed part. $\perp\!\!\!\perp$ is independence, and $\mathbf{X} \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|S$ is conditional independence given $S$. $z$ and $z'$ range over $\{1, \ldots, K\}$. Every numbered result is a statement about this population law; no target is asymptotic. The paper does not define ‘sharp bounds’. The targets use the usual meaning: the infimum and supremum of the target parameter over all joint laws of the potential variables and $Z$ that satisfy the assumptions and induce the given law of the observables $(Y, S, Z)$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, sentence ‘We observe that the bounds for all treatment conditions have overlapping regions, in both outcome variables’, as printed (Figure 1, Panels D–E; Figure 2, Panels D–E); the exact intervals are the validator's reconstruction from the deposited data and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: pp. 578–579 (PDF pp. 7–8); Figure 1, p. 577 (PDF p. 6); Figure 2, p. 585 (PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted: Section 3, foot of p. 578 and top of p. 579] “We also report sharp bounds for the average potential outcomes among subjects who would pass the manipulation check regardless of treatment assignment. [...] Panel D depicts our results imputing the lower bound, whereas Panel E shows our estimates imputing the upper bound. We observe that the bounds for all treatment conditions have overlapping regions, in both outcome variables, making it impossible to fully differentiate results across the treatments. The bounds are largely uninformative, suggesting the fundamental uncertainty induced by attempting to estimate effects among the subpopulation of subjects who would always pass the manipulation check. If these effects are indeed the inferential target of the researcher, very little is revealed by the experimental data, and dropping subjects may introduce serious bias of unknown sign and magnitude (as any values within the range of the bounds are compatible with the experimental data).” [Formal reading of the overlap claim] For each of the two outcomes and each treatment $t \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ (90–90, 90–70, 90–45), let $I_t = [\ell_t, u_t]$ run from the estimated lower bound (Panel D) to the estimated upper bound (Panel E). The printed claim is that, for both outcomes, the three intervals overlap: $I_s \cap I_t 
e \emptyset$ for all $s, t$ (or, in the stronger reading, $I_1 \cap I_2 \cap I_3 
e \emptyset$). [Counterexample: the unweighted bounds of Figure 2, reconstructed exactly by the validator from the deposited data with the authors' own trimming rule] Counts in the three arms (90–90, 90–70, 90–45): $N = (544, 538, 533)$, failures $(35, 182, 40)$, passers $(509, 356, 493)$; among passers, ‘prefer nuclear use’ equals 1 for $(61, 162, 327)$ and ‘approve nuclear use’ equals 1 for $(192, 188, 324)$. Failure rates $f_t$ = failures$/N$: $f_1 = 35/544$, $f_2 = 91/269$, $f_3 = 40/533$. Trimming proportions $\mathrm{trim}_t = \sum_{s 
e t} f_s/(1 - f_t)$: $32239072/72978893$, $10871635/51611456$, $31403827/72143648$. Rule of the authors' deposited helper: sort the $n_t$ passers' binary outcomes of arm $t$ in increasing order; the lower bound is the mean of the observations $j$ with $j/n_t < 1 - \mathrm{trim}_t$ and the upper bound the mean of those with $j/n_t > \mathrm{trim}_t$. Retained counts: lower tail $(284, 281, 278)$, upper tail $(285, 282, 279)$. For ‘prefer nuclear use’ this gives $I_1 = [0, 61/285]$, $I_2 = [87/281, 162/282] = [87/281, 27/47]$ and $I_3 = [112/278, 279/279] = [56/139, 1]$ (in percent: $[0, 21.403509]$, $[30.960854, 57.446809]$, $[40.287770, 100]$). Then $87/281 - 61/285 = 7654/80085 > 0$ and $56/139 - 61/285 = 7481/39615 > 0$, so $I_1 \cap I_2 = \emptyset$ and $I_1 \cap I_3 = \emptyset$: the preference intervals do not all overlap, under either reading of the claim.

canonical_claim.note: P010-N011 is rated an error, Moderate, of kind interpretive. It is a target because it rests on an exact refutation (validator evidence type: Lean proof; validate/P010-N011/v1/artifact/check.lean, and the second validator's exact certificate in validate/P010-N011/v2/artifact/), so this target and P010-T2 have priority 2. The printed sentence is an empirical description, not a numbered result; it is transcribed here in full and no separate target of kind result_touched_by_finding is listed. The intervals are plug-in estimates, not population parameters; the counts are inputs from the deposited data (abp_replication_data.csv) and cannot be derived in Lean, but the retained counts and the endpoints follow from the counts by the stated rule. ‘Overlap’ refers to the intervals from the Panel D to the Panel E estimates, not to the vertical confidence bars. The weighted Figure 1 shows the same separation at graphical precision (preference about $[0, 19.7]$, $[41.5, 66.8]$, $[26.5, 100]$ percent, read from the drawing operands of the PDF); those values are approximate, the PSV weights being withheld, and are not part of the target. The verdict is ‘confirmed in part’: ‘largely uninformative’ and ‘very little is revealed’ are qualitative and are not refuted.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, the overlap sentence and the two sentences after it, corrected
canonical_claim.location: pp. 578–579 (PDF pp. 7–8); Figure 2, Panels D–E, p. 585 (PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected text, from Sol's smallest repair; it replaces the overlap sentence transcribed in P010-T1 and qualifies the next two] “The estimated approval bounds overlap across all three treatments. For preference, the estimated upper bound for 90-90 is below the estimated lower bounds for both 90-70 and 90-45, while the bounds for 90-70 and 90-45 overlap. Thus the estimated preference bounds distinguish equal effectiveness from a nuclear advantage, although the bounds remain wide and do not fully order all three treatments or determine precise effect magnitudes. Sampling uncertainty is distinct from the width of these bounds.” [Formal content, for the unweighted bounds of Figure 2] Counts in the three arms (90–90, 90–70, 90–45): $N = (544, 538, 533)$, failures $(35, 182, 40)$, passers $(509, 356, 493)$; among passers, ‘prefer nuclear use’ equals 1 for $(61, 162, 327)$ and ‘approve nuclear use’ equals 1 for $(192, 188, 324)$. Failure rates $f_t$ = failures$/N$: $f_1 = 35/544$, $f_2 = 91/269$, $f_3 = 40/533$. Trimming proportions $\mathrm{trim}_t = \sum_{s \ne t} f_s/(1 - f_t)$: $32239072/72978893$, $10871635/51611456$, $31403827/72143648$. Rule of the authors' deposited helper: sort the $n_t$ passers' binary outcomes of arm $t$ in increasing order; the lower bound is the mean of the observations $j$ with $j/n_t < 1 - \mathrm{trim}_t$ and the upper bound the mean of those with $j/n_t > \mathrm{trim}_t$. Retained counts: lower tail $(284, 281, 278)$, upper tail $(285, 282, 279)$. Then: (a) approval: the three intervals are $[0, 64/95]$, $[113/281, 2/3]$ and $[109/278, 1]$, and $1/2$ lies in all three; (b) preference: $I_1 = [0, 61/285]$, $I_2 = [87/281, 27/47]$, $I_3 = [56/139, 1]$; $1/2 \in I_2 \cap I_3$; and $61/285 < 87/281$, $61/285 < 56/139$, so $I_1$ lies wholly below $I_2$ and $I_3$; (c) the estimated bounds on the differences of the always-passer means have positive lower endpoints: $87/281 - 61/285 = 7654/80085 > 0$ (90–70 minus 90–90) and $56/139 - 61/285 = 7481/39615 > 0$ (90–45 minus 90–90); (d) the same holds with exact fractional trimming of the passers' empirical distributions: with $q = 1 - f_1 - f_2 - f_3 = 40739821/77997088 > 0$ and $a_t$ the share of arm $t$ that passes with outcome 1 ($a_1 = 61/544$, $a_2 = 162/538$, $a_3 = 327/533$), the bounds $[\max(0, (a_t - \sum_{s \ne t} f_s)/q), \min(1, a_t/q)]$ are $[0, 8745997/40739821]$, $[12614477/40739821, 23486112/40739821]$ and $[16448045/40739821, 1]$, with gaps $3868480/40739821 > 0$ and $7702048/40739821 > 0$ between the upper endpoint of the first and the lower endpoints of the second and third.

canonical_claim.note: The formal content of the corrected claim, as the brief requires for an interpretive finding that rests on an exact refutation. Parts (a)–(c) and the two gaps of (d) are already proved in the validator's check.lean (norm_num and linarith on rationals); the formula in (d) for binary outcomes is derived in Section ‘Check with exact fractional trimming’ of the artifact. Part (d) shows that the conclusion does not depend on the whole-observation cut-off convention of the deposited helper (finding P010-E017, a finding about code, which has no target). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, displayed bounds, as printed (outer conditional means without $S = 1$)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted: p. 575 (PDF p. 4)] PROPOSITION 1. Suppose that $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] > 0$ and that $Y$ is continuous with unbounded support. Let $Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}(.)$ denote the conditional quantile function of $Y$ given $Z = z$ and $S = 1$. Then, sharp bounds for $\mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$ are given by $$\mathrm{E}\left[Y \,\middle|\, Y \le Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}\left(1 - \sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' 
e z}  rac{\Pr[S = 0|Z = z']}{\Pr[S = 1|Z = z]}ight), Z = zight] \le \mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] \le \mathrm{E}\left[Y \,\middle|\, Y \ge Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}\left(\sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' 
e z}  rac{\Pr[S = 0|Z = z']}{\Pr[S = 1|Z = z]}ight), Z = zight]$$ when $\sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' 
e z}  rac{\Pr[S=0|Z=z']}{\Pr[S=1|Z=z]} < 1$, else these bounds are given by $-\infty \le \mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] \le \infty$. [The same outer conditioning event, without $S = 1$, recurs in the last display of the proof, p. 580 (PDF p. 9), transcribed in P010-T15.] [Counterexample, from the validator: two laws with the same law of $(Y, S, Z)$] $K = 2$. $Z$ is independent of all potential variables with $\Pr[Z = 1] = \Pr[Z = 2] = 1/2$. Let $W$ denote an exponential variable of rate 1 and $V$ a variable with density $e^{-2|v|}$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The strata are: with probability $1/4$, $(S(1), S(2)) = (1, 1)$ and $Y(1) \sim -W$ in the lower model, $Y(1) \sim W$ in the upper model; with probability $1/4$, $(S(1), S(2)) = (1, 0)$ and $Y(1) \sim W$ in the lower model, $Y(1) \sim -W$ in the upper model; with probability $1/2$, $(S(1), S(2)) = (0, 1)$ and $Y(1) \sim V$ in both models. $Y(2)$ has density $e^{-|y|}/2$ and is independent of the stratum and of $Y(1)$. $Y = Y(Z)$, $S = S(Z)$. Then, in both models: (a) Assumptions 1–3 hold; $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = 1] = 1/4 > 0$; $Y$ is continuous with support $\mathbb{R}$ and all moments finite; the two models induce the same law of $(Y, S, Z)$; (b) $\Pr[S = 1|Z = 1] = 1/2$, $\Pr[S = 1|Z = 2] = 3/4$, so for $z = 1$ the ratio is $\Pr[S = 0|Z = 2]/\Pr[S = 1|Z = 1] = (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2 < 1$; given $Z = 1$ and $S = 1$, $Y$ has density $e^{-|y|}/2$, so $Q_{Y|Z=1,S=1}(1/2) = 0$; (c) the printed lower expression is $\mathrm{E}[Y|Y \le 0, Z = 1] = (-3/8)/(1/2) = -3/4$ and the printed upper expression is $\mathrm{E}[Y|Y \ge 0, Z = 1] = 3/4$; (d) the target $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|S(1) = S(2) = 1]$ equals $-1$ in the lower model and $1$ in the upper model. The printed inequalities assert $-3/4 \le -1$ in the lower model and $1 \le 3/4$ in the upper model; both are false, each by $1/4$. (e) With $S = 1$ added, $\mathrm{E}[Y|Y \le 0, Z = 1, S = 1] = -1$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|Y \ge 0, Z = 1, S = 1] = 1$: the interval $[-1, 1]$ of P010-T4, attained at its endpoints by the two models.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$Y$, $S$, $Z$, $Y(z)$, $S(z)$ and Assumptions 1–3: standing assumptions, pp. 573–574 (PDF pp. 2–3).] [Quantile function: inside Proposition 1, p. 575 (PDF p. 4)] “Let $Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}(.)$ denote the conditional quantile function of $Y$ given $Z = z$ and $S = 1$.” [Sentence after the Proposition, p. 575] “Assuming that $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] > 0$ ensures that $\mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$ exists and continuity of $Y$ ensures that the quantile function is well defined. As with Lee (2009)'s bounds, even when $Y$ is discrete, then bounds can be constructed simply by trimming the observations associated with the upper or lower $\sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' \ne z} \frac{\Pr[S=0|Z=z']}{\Pr[S=1|Z=z]}$th proportions of the empirical distributions of subjects who pass the manipulation check under treatment and control.” [‘Sharp bounds’ is not defined in the paper; see the standing assumptions for the meaning used.]
canonical_claim.note: P010-E001 is rated an error, Minor: the sentence after the Proposition and the deposited code trim passers only, and no reported number changes. The example has an interior quantile, full real support and finite moments, so it does not turn on ties, endpoints or the existence of means. The validator's check_exact.py confirms every value in exact arithmetic ($\Pr[Y \le 0|Z = 1] = 1/2$, $\mathrm{E}[Y\mathbf{1}\{Y \le 0\}|Z = 1] = -3/8$).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, corrected: the branch with trimming ratio below one
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected Proposition 1, finite branch. Changes from the printed statement (transcribed in P010-T3): $S = 1$ is added to both outer conditioning events; the integrability that the paper leaves to its regularity conditions is written out; the meaning of ‘sharp’ is written out. The quantile cut-offs, the trimming share and the estimand are unchanged. The else-branch is corrected in P010-T6.] Under Assumptions 1–3 (Assumption 3 as corrected in P010-T17), fix $z \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ and write $A = \{S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1\}$ and $r_z = \sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' \ne z} \frac{\Pr[S = 0|Z = z']}{\Pr[S = 1|Z = z]}$. Suppose that $\Pr[A] > 0$, that $Y$ is continuous (what is used: the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $Z = z$ and $S = 1$ has no atoms), that $\mathrm{E}[|Y|\,|\,Z = z, S = 1] < \infty$, and that $r_z < 1$. Let $Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}(.)$ denote the conditional quantile function of $Y$ given $Z = z$ and $S = 1$. Then: (i) $$\mathrm{E}\left[Y \,\middle|\, Y \le Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}(1 - r_z), Z = z, S = 1\right] \le \mathrm{E}[Y(z)|A] \le \mathrm{E}\left[Y \,\middle|\, Y \ge Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}(r_z), Z = z, S = 1\right];$$ (ii) the bounds are sharp, and attained: there is a joint law of $(Y(1), \ldots, Y(K), S(1), \ldots, S(K), Z)$ that satisfies Assumptions 1–3 and $\Pr[A] > 0$, induces the given law of $(Y, S, Z)$, and has $\mathrm{E}[Y(z)|A]$ equal to the left-hand side of (i), and another such law for which it equals the right-hand side. [Equivalent form, from the validator] With $p_k = \Pr[S = 1|Z = k]$, $L = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K}(1 - p_k)$ and $Q_z = Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}$: $p_z(1 - r_z) = L$, so $r_z < 1$ if and only if $L > 0$, and the bounds are $\frac{p_z}{L}\int_0^{L/p_z} Q_z(u)\,du \le \mathrm{E}[Y(z)|A] \le \frac{p_z}{L}\int_{1-L/p_z}^{1} Q_z(u)\,du$; when $r_z = 0$ both equal $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = z, S = 1]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$Y$, $S$, $Z$, $Y(z)$, $S(z)$ and Assumptions 1–3: standing assumptions, pp. 573–574 (PDF pp. 2–3).] [Quantile function: inside Proposition 1, p. 575 (PDF p. 4)] “Let $Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}(.)$ denote the conditional quantile function of $Y$ given $Z = z$ and $S = 1$.” [Sentence after the Proposition, p. 575] “Assuming that $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] > 0$ ensures that $\mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$ exists and continuity of $Y$ ensures that the quantile function is well defined. As with Lee (2009)'s bounds, even when $Y$ is discrete, then bounds can be constructed simply by trimming the observations associated with the upper or lower $\sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' \ne z} \frac{\Pr[S=0|Z=z']}{\Pr[S=1|Z=z]}$th proportions of the empirical distributions of subjects who pass the manipulation check under treatment and control.” [‘Sharp bounds’ is not defined in the paper; see the standing assumptions for the meaning used.]
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair: add $S = 1$ to both outer conditioning events in Proposition 1 and to the right-hand conditional expectation in the proof's final bound; leave the quantile cut-offs and the target estimand unchanged. This target is also the paper's headline result P010-H4 in its correct form (the finding is Minor, so the printed statement is not a separate target). The validator's derivation (Section 3) proves (i) from the union bound $\Pr[A] \ge L$, the rearrangement inequality $(W - q)(\mathbf{1}_B - \mathbf{1}_T) \ge 0$ and the monotonicity of tail averages in the retained mass, and proves (ii) by an explicit construction with disjoint failure sets. Two hypotheses are not in the printed statement: the integrability condition, which the paper leaves to the ‘suitable regularity conditions (e.g., finite third moments, continuity)’ of Section 2.1 (clarity note P010-E003: positivity of $\Pr[A]$ does not by itself make the mean exist); and the explicit meaning of ‘sharp’. The printed hypothesis of unbounded support is not used on this branch. The integral form also covers outcomes with atoms, by fractional trimming at the cut-off, which is how the paragraph after the Proposition extends the bounds to discrete $Y$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, the else-branch (‘else these bounds are given by $-\infty \le \ldots \le \infty$’), as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 575 (PDF p. 4); matching clauses of the proof, p. 580 (PDF p. 9)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: Proposition 1, p. 575 (PDF p. 4), transcribed in full in P010-T3] Under the hypotheses “$\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] > 0$ and that $Y$ is continuous with unbounded support”, sharp bounds for $\mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$ are given by the trimmed means “when $\sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' \ne z} \frac{\Pr[S=0|Z=z']}{\Pr[S=1|Z=z]} < 1$, else these bounds are given by $-\infty \le \mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] \le \infty$.” [The two matching clauses of the proof, p. 580 (PDF p. 9), transcribed in P010-T13 and P010-T15] “else the upper bound is infinite.” [Counterexample, from the adjudicating validator] $K = 2$. $B$, $X$, $V$, $Z$ are mutually independent: $\Pr(B = 1) = 1/3$; $\Pr(Z = 1) = \Pr(Z = 2) = 1/2$; $X$ has density $b(x) = 30x^2(1 - x)^2$ on $(0, 1)$; $V$ has density $h(v) = \frac{5}{2(1 + |v|)^6}$ on $\mathbb{R}$. $S(1) = S(2) = B$; $Y(1) = Y(2) = X$ if $B = 1$ and $Y(1) = Y(2) = V$ if $B = 0$; $Y = Y(Z)$, $S = S(Z)$. Then: (a) Assumptions 1–3 hold and $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = 1] = 1/3 > 0$; (b) $Y$ has density $g = \frac13 b + \frac23 h$, continuous and strictly positive on $\mathbb{R}$, with $\Pr(Y > R) = \Pr(Y < -R) = \frac{1}{3(1 + R)^5}$ for $R \ge 1$, so $Y$ is continuous with support unbounded in both directions; $\mathrm{E}[Y] = 1/6$, $\mathrm{E}[Y^2] = 13/63$, $\mathrm{E}|Y|^3 = 19/84$; (c) $\Pr[S = 1|Z = z] = 1/3$ and the ratio is $(2/3)/(1/3) = 2 \ge 1$ for $z = 1, 2$, so the printed else-branch applies and asserts that $-\infty$ and $\infty$ are sharp; (d) in every joint law of $(Y(1), Y(2), S(1), S(2), Z)$ that satisfies Assumptions 1–3 with $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = 1] > 0$ and induces this law of $(Y, S, Z)$, $0 < \mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = 1] < 1$ for $z = 1, 2$, because $\{S(1) = S(2) = 1\} \subseteq \{S(z) = 1\}$ and $\Pr(Y \notin (0, 1), S = 1|Z = z) = 0$. Hence $-\infty$ and $\infty$ are not sharp bounds. (e) The sharp infimum and supremum are $0$ and $1$: for $0 < t < 1$ let $q = F(t) = 10t^3 - 15t^4 + 6t^5$; the law with stratum probabilities $(q/3, (1 - q)/3, (1 - q)/3, (1 + q)/3)$ for $(S(1), S(2)) = (1,1), (1,0), (0,1), (0,0)$, always-passer outcome density $b\mathbf{1}_{(0,t)}/q$ for $Y(1)$ and $Y(2)$, outcome density $b\mathbf{1}_{[t,1)}/(1 - q)$ for the arm in which a one-arm passer passes, and $h$ wherever a subject fails (outcomes drawn independently given the stratum, $Z$ independent and uniform on $\{1, 2\}$), satisfies Assumptions 1–3, induces the same law of $(Y, S, Z)$ and has $\mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = 1] = \frac{t(15/2 - 12t + 5t^2)}{10 - 15t + 6t^2} \in (0, t)$; replacing $(0, t)$ by $(1 - t, 1)$ and $[t, 1)$ by $(0, 1 - t]$ gives one minus this value.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$Y$, $S$, $Z$, $Y(z)$, $S(z)$ and Assumptions 1–3: standing assumptions, pp. 573–574 (PDF pp. 2–3).] [Quantile function: inside Proposition 1, p. 575 (PDF p. 4)] “Let $Q_{Y|Z=z,S=1}(.)$ denote the conditional quantile function of $Y$ given $Z = z$ and $S = 1$.” [Sentence after the Proposition, p. 575] “Assuming that $\Pr[S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1] > 0$ ensures that $\mathrm{E}[Y(z)|S(1) = S(2) = \cdots = S(K) = 1]$ exists and continuity of $Y$ ensures that the quantile function is well defined. As with Lee (2009)'s bounds, even when $Y$ is discrete, then bounds can be constructed simply by trimming the observations associated with the upper or lower $\sum_{z' \in \{1,\ldots,K\}:z' \ne z} \frac{\Pr[S=0|Z=z']}{\Pr[S=1|Z=z]}$th proportions of the empirical distributions of subjects who pass the manipulation check under treatment and control.” [‘Sharp bounds’ is not defined in the paper; see the standing assumptions for the meaning used.]
canonical_claim.note: P010-E002 is rated an error, Minor: the infinite interval is still a valid outer bound and no simulation design or application ratio reaches this branch (the largest population ratio in Table 1 is $2/3$). What fails is the claimed sharpness. Two validators confirmed it with different examples and the adjudication (status settled) supplies the one transcribed here, with every moment checked in exact arithmetic (check.py). The raisers' simpler example has passers uniform on $(0, 1)$ and failers standard normal, with pass rate $2/5$. The printed hypothesis ‘unbounded support’ is satisfied here in the strongest reading (full real support).
